original_question: Classify which polling systems, in terms of their service disciplines, visit disciplines, and scheduling disciplines, have the following asymptotic property: as switch-over times become large, the system exhibits the same deterministic limiting behaviour discussed in the paper, including in settings with dynamic visit orders rather than a fixed pre-determined queue order.
target_in_paper: The draft is targeting the unnumbered related open problem in the last paragraph of §4.2: after discussing Conjecture 4.2 and Open problem 2, the authors ask for "the classification of polling systems in terms of service, visit and scheduling disciplines, which exhibit the discussed behaviour," explicitly extending the discussion to systems with dynamic visit orders. citeturn10view2
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the paper's classification focus, the large-switch-over-time regime, the deterministic limiting behaviour, and the fact that the paper explicitly raises the dynamic-visit-order case rather than restricting attention to a fixed predetermined cyclic order. citeturn10view2turn9view0
missing_details: The paper's asymptotic regime is not merely "large switch-over times": the switch-over times are deterministic and tend to infinity; in the cyclic results of §4.1 the scaling is by the total switch-over time S while keeping the ratios of the individual switch-over times fixed. citeturn8view0turn9view0

The ambient model is an N-queue, single-server polling system; the nearby notation uses queues Qi, service times Bi, switch-over times Si, total switch-over time S, loads ρi=λiE[Bi], and total load ρ=∑iρi. citeturn7view0

The phrase "the discussed behaviour" should be made explicit: in §4.1 it means convergence to a deterministic cyclic system, manifested for example by scaled queue lengths at polling instants becoming deterministic; for branching-type cyclic systems with Poisson arrivals, the scaled waiting time Wi/S has the explicit limit in Eq. (7). citeturn8view0turn9view0

The draft does not separate the two scopes that the paper keeps distinct nearby: Conjecture 4.2 concerns cyclic systems with general renewal arrivals, whereas the final dynamic-visit-order discussion is stated for systems with Poisson arrivals and is supported there only by numerical and heuristic evidence. citeturn9view0turn10view2

The dynamic-order paragraph adds an important implicit condition absent from the draft: the analogous limit theorems are conjectured to hold when the switch-overs perform a regulating effect. The paper mentions this condition heuristically but does not formalize it. citeturn10view2

If the question is to be fully stand-alone, it should say that "dynamic visit orders" means there is no predetermined order in which the queues are served; the paper's concrete example is the rule that the server switches next to the longest queue. citeturn10view2

No algebraic data such as ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree restrictions, or nilpotency are relevant here; the missing stand-alone details are instead the stochastic-model assumptions, the scaling, and the precise meaning of the deterministic limit. citeturn7view0turn10view2
refined_question: Classify the N-queue single-server polling systems, in terms of their service, visit, and scheduling disciplines, for which deterministic switch-over times Si tending to infinity yield the deterministic large-switch-over-time behaviour discussed in §4: under the standard scaling by the total switch-over time S (and, in the fixed cyclic case, with fixed ratios Si/S), the system approaches a deterministic limiting regime, as manifested by scaled queue lengths at polling instants becoming deterministic and by analogous large-switch-over-time waiting-time limit theorems. In particular, in the Poisson-arrival setting singled out in the paper, determine whether and under what precise conditions this remains true for systems with dynamic visit orders, i.e. with no predetermined queue order (for example, when the server moves next to the longest queue), as conjectured when the switch-overs exert a regulating effect. citeturn8view0turn9view0turn10view2
justification: The draft does not best match Open problem 2 itself, whose exact statement is only to prove Conjecture 4.2 for cyclic polling systems with general renewal arrivals. Because your draft asks for a classification by service, visit, and scheduling disciplines and explicitly includes dynamic visit orders, it aligns most closely with the separate unnumbered open problem in the last paragraph of §4.2. The meaning of "the discussed behaviour" in that sentence is supplied by the immediately preceding context: the deterministic-limit interpretation in §4.1 and Conjecture 4.2 in §4.2. citeturn9view0turn10view2turn8view0
